Learning intention: I am learning to compare unit prices and justify a purchasing choice
Teaching support: Unit price puts different pack sizes on the same basis. Check whether the cheaper option also meets the need. Worked example: 4 for $10 = $2.50 each; 6 for $12 = $2 each
Release status: Demo review only; every demo activity is unlocked
Reasoning example and solution: Pack A: 4 notebooks for $34.00. Pack B: 6 for $49.50. Which comparison correctly identifies the lower unit price? Solution: B is cheaper: $8.25 each versus A: $8.50 each.. Divide each pack's price by its quantity. B is $0.25 cheaper per notebook; total pack price alone does not compare equal quantities.
Application example and solution: 8 notebooks cost $44.00. What is the cost of one notebook in dollars? Solution: 5.5. Divide the pack price by 8: $44.00 ÷ 8 = $5.50.

Title: Plan an expedition budget
Learning intention: I am learning to choose representations to solve a multi-step rational-number problem
Teaching support: Build a calculation from the information, estimate, solve, then interpret the answer. Worked example: 3 supplies at $4.50 plus $2 delivery = $15.50
Student unlock requirement: Pass every earlier weekly quiz with at least 80%
Release status: Demo review only; every demo activity is unlocked
Reasoning example and solution: You have $61. Buy 8 supplies at $8.75 each and pay one delivery fee of $5. Which model gives money remaining? Solution: 61 − (8 × 8.75 + 5). Multiply quantity by unit price, add delivery once, then subtract the full cost from the budget.
Application example and solution: You have $220. You buy 11 kits at $7.50 each. How many dollars remain? Solution: 137.5. Kits cost 11 × $7.50. Subtract this cost from $220.

Title: Model signed changes
Learning intention: I am learning to interpret positive and negative changes in context
Teaching support: Choose zero as a reference and translate each change into a signed operation. Worked example: A lift starts at −3, rises 8, then descends 2 → floor 3
Release status: Demo review only; every demo activity is unlocked
Reasoning example and solution: A lift starts at floor −8, rises 11 floors, then descends 5. Which model finds the final floor? Solution: −8 + 11 − 5. Use the signed starting position, add the rise and subtract the descent. Distance travelled would be 16, a different quantity.
Application example and solution: A lift starts at floor -8, rises 11 floors, then descends to floor -5. How many floors does it descend? Solution: 8. After rising, the lift is at floor 3. The descent from there to -5 is 3 − (-5) = 8 floors.

Title: Justify a model and check a solution
Learning intention: I am learning to select a calculation and explain why it matches the situation
Teaching support: A good model accounts for the quantities and their order. Check the result against the context. Worked example: A $60 bag is 20% off, then $5 delivery: 60 × 0.8 + 5 = $53
Release status: Demo review only; every demo activity is unlocked
Reasoning example and solution: 65% of 220 students buy a ticket costing $5.50. Which model gives ticket revenue? Solution: 220 × 0.65 × 5.5. Convert the attendance percentage to a decimal to find the number buying tickets, then multiply by the ticket price.
Application example and solution: 60% of 220 students attend an event and pay $5.50 each. Total event costs are $55. What is the profit in dollars? Solution: 671. Attendance = 220 × 0.6 = 132. Revenue = 132 × $5.50 = $726. Subtract costs of $55 to get $671.
